column3: Personal daily load
column5: Carry a daily target of points and visits and work through the day handed to them.
column6: Capacity is my day - how full it is, how far I drive, whether I finish by my hard stop. 'Productivity' can feel like a treadmill measured in points.
column7: A day that is full on paper can be impossible once geography and real visit times are counted.
column8: Keep control over my own limits and hard stop. Offload nothing that overrides them.
column9: A full but doable day that ends on time.

column3: Availability and time off
column5: Declare working days, PTO, and non-working days.
column6: This is my boundary with work, and I expect it honored once I have entered it.
column7: PTO is entered and then scheduled over anyway, which reads as the system not seeing them.
column8: Keep ownership of my availability. Offload only the honoring of it, never the overriding.
column9: Declared time off is never booked against.

column3: Working pattern
column5: Set preferred days, start time, lunch, documentation block, and any split shift.
column6: These are my life - childcare, commute, the shape of my day - not preferences to be traded freely.
column7: A scheduler who does not know me rebuilds my day wrong and I have to fight to fix it.
column8: Keep my rhythm. Offload the stable, documented parts so a covering scheduler still gets it right.
column9: A schedule that fits the shape of my day without me defending it every week.

column3: Flex and elasticity
column5: Decide, day by day, how much I will bend my pattern for a squeeze-in.
column6: Flexing is a favor I choose to give, not an obligation; being volunteered without being asked breaks trust fast.
column7: Assumptions about my flexibility get baked into the schedule without anyone checking with me.
column8: Keep the choice to say yes or no. This should never be assumed on my behalf.
column9: I am asked, not told, when the schedule needs me to stretch.

column3: Hard stop
column5: Hold a firm end time for the day.
column6: Non-negotiable - childcare or a second obligation - and a schedule that ignores it simply fails.
column7: Hard stops are treated as soft until a late visit forces the issue.
column8: Keep the hard stop absolute. Offload only its enforcement.
column9: No visit is ever placed past my hard stop.

column3: Route and mileage
column5: Drive the sequence of visits handed to them across the day.
column6: A bad route is unpaid windshield time; I re-order it in my head on the drive because the paper order ignores reality.
column7: Routes optimized on paper miss the real facts - parking, a patient never ready early, a slow building.
column8: Keep the on-the-ground re-order. Offload a base route that starts closer to reality.
column9: A route that reflects how the day actually drives, not just the map.

column3: Patient and caregiver reality
column5: Discover and work with the real patient and caregiver constraints at the door.
column6: I am the sensor - I learn the dementia caregiver window, the refusal, the fact that the map is wrong. It lives with me first.
column7: What I learn at the door does not flow back into the schedule, so the same wrong assumption repeats.
column8: Keep the reading of the situation. Offload a clean way to feed it back so it sticks.
column9: What I learn once changes the schedule for good.

column3: Continuity
column5: Prefer to keep seeing my own patients across the episode.
column6: Continuity is clinical quality and relationship, not a scheduling nicety; I know my patients and catch changes a stranger would miss.
column7: Continuity breaks under coverage pressure and no one sees the clinical cost.
column8: Keep me on my patients where possible. Offload the flag when continuity is about to break.
column9: I follow my patients through the episode.

column3: Visit match and acuity
column5: Receive visits matched to my discipline, skill, and competency.
column6: Being handed a visit beyond my competency is unsafe; being underused is a waste of my training. I notice both.
column7: Mismatches happen when the competency data is thin, and I absorb the risk.
column8: Keep me from unsafe matches. Offload the routine matching to trusted data.
column9: Every visit is one I am the right and safe clinician for.

column3: Day-before confirmation
column5: Often the one who calls the patient to confirm tomorrow's visit.
column6: A chore that saves me a wasted trip; I would happily hand off the reminder and keep the call that surfaces a real change.
column7: The confirmation call is mine on top of a full day of visits and documentation.
column8: Keep the judgment call. Offload the routine reminder.
column9: Tomorrow's visits are confirmed without it costing my evening.

column3: On-my-way notice
column5: Text or call the patient when I am en route.
column6: A small courtesy that smooths the visit and settles the patient before I arrive.
column7: One more manual touch during the drive when my hands are full.
column8: Keep the personal touch when it matters. Offload the routine on-my-way text.
column9: Patients know I am coming without me stopping to tell each one.

column3: Reschedule at the door
column5: When a visit fails, rebook it on the spot with the patient or family.
column6: Relational recovery I own better than the office because I am standing right there with the family.
column7: What I agree at the door does not always make it back into the schedule cleanly.
column8: Keep the on-the-spot rebook. Offload getting it recorded without a second call.
column9: A door-step reschedule that holds without office rework.

column3: Coordination time
column5: Absorb the non-visit coordination work across the day.
column6: Invisible, unpaid-feeling work - roughly forty-five minutes a day - that eats into my documentation and my own time.
column7: It is never counted, so it never gets resourced or reduced.
column8: Keep the parts that need my judgment. Offload the mechanical coordination.
column9: Less time on the phone and more on patients and charting.

column1: Clinicians are not interchangeable capacity. Each carries drivers - some chosen, some fixed by their life, some shaped by history with the branch - that determine how they respond to scheduling, coverage requests, and efficiency gains. Some of these are not malleable; the system has to work around them rather than expect them to change. The goal is not to convert every clinician into a maximizer, but to set realistic expectations for each and to read which drivers are fixed, which were shaped by past experience, and which can still be moved.

column3: Motivated to earn, often on per-visit pay. Wants a full, dense day and more visits when they are available.
column5: More capacity for themselves - efficiency means they can fit additional visits and take home more.
column7: The branch's elastic surge capacity: first to say yes to extra visits and same-day adds when the work is workable.
column8: Partly
column9: Feed them the extra visits fast and in a clean route. They are the release valve - keep a pipeline of workable adds flowing to them.

column3: Meets targets reliably; values work-life balance over maximizing volume.
column5: Not more visits - the same rate delivered with less stress, better care, or an earlier finish.
column7: Steady, dependable base load; will not routinely absorb extra and should not be counted on for surge.
column8: Fixed
column9: Return efficiency to them as quality or time, not as more visits. Expect reliable throughput, not stretch - and be genuinely OK with that.

column3: Deep attachment to their zips, patients, and known routes; reluctant to cross territory.
column5: Efficiency inside their area is welcome; it does not change their reluctance to leave it.
column7: Strong within territory, resistant to cross-coverage - a gap when demand shifts outside their zone.
column8: Partly
column9: Treat their territory as the default, not a limit to fight. Make cross-coverage genuinely workable - a tight route, a worthwhile block - before asking, and ask fairly.

column3: Carries historical frustration - past cancellations that took the branch an hour or two to backfill, leaving them with dead time.
column5: Skeptical that gains are real; has been promised workable coverage before and been left waiting.
column7: Withholds flexibility to protect against wasted time; declines extra and cross-coverage on principle until trust returns.
column8: Shapeable
column9: Rebuild trust with proof: fast, workable replacements delivered in minutes, not hours. Reliability across several cycles moves this clinician; promises do not.

column3: Hard stop, childcare, split shift, fixed lunch - the pattern is their life, not a preference.
column5: Efficiency that respects the pattern helps; efficiency that assumes they will flex it does not.
column7: Predictable and bounded; the pattern is a hard constraint that reshapes any day built for them.
column8: Fixed
column9: Treat the pattern as a hard rule, not a lever. Never schedule past a hard stop or across a fixed block; build the day inside their real edges.

column3: Genuinely adaptable; says yes, adjusts, covers - the easy one to schedule.
column5: Happy to gain efficiency and to help; rarely counts the cost to themselves.
column7: High willingness to flex and cover; quietly becomes the branch's default yes.
column8: Shapeable
column9: Protect them from being over-tapped. Rotate the asks so the willing do not burn out and harden into the scarred archetype - the most common way a branch loses its flex.

column3: Still ramping or building confidence; careful on higher acuity and unfamiliar territory.
column5: Efficiency helps once they trust it; too much too fast raises anxiety.
column7: Real capacity that is not yet full; over-loading or mis-matching acuity risks a safety or retention problem.
column8: Partly
column9: Ramp deliberately, match to appropriate acuity, and grow the load as competence and confidence build. Do not treat ramped headcount as full capacity.

Negative resting patterns (what hardens a branch)
column7: Positive resting patterns (what a healthy branch settles into)

column1: -  Slow-replacement scar: after a cancellation the branch historically took one to two hours to offer a workable replacement, so clinicians stopped trusting that saying yes would be worth their time. -  Hoarding the willing: the same few flexible clinicians get every coverage ask, burn out, and harden into a no - shrinking the flex pool over time. -  Territory entrenchment: cross-coverage is only ever asked in a crisis, so the habit never forms and leaving one's zone feels abnormal. -  Points-as-treadmill: productivity is framed only as more, so balanced clinicians disengage from efficiency entirely.
column7: -  Fast, workable backfill: replacements are offered in minutes with a real route, so clinicians trust the branch and take them. -  Fair rotation of asks: coverage requests are spread across the team, so no one clinician hardens from over-use. -  Earners fed surge: maximizers reliably receive the extra work, giving the branch dependable elastic capacity. -  Efficiency returned as choice: gains are offered as take-more or finish-earlier, so both earners and balance-seekers opt in on their own terms.

column1: Change-management read: you cannot schedule your way out of a trust deficit. Name the negative resting patterns in a branch first - most reluctance to cover or take extra is a rational response to past inefficiency, not a personality flaw. Set expectations per archetype, prove reliability before asking for stretch, and accept that a balanced clinician who meets their role is a success, not a conversion target.
